hints: Look at what group has been added to benzene to make phenylethanone, a $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$ ketone. What acyl fragment must be supplied?
Recall which reactive acyl compound plus which Lewis acid catalyst is used to generate the acylium electrophile for Friedel-Crafts acylation.
walkthrough:
Spot the acylation pattern**
You start with benzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$, and end with $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$. The ring has gained a $\text{COCH}_3$ group. That is the classic sign of Friedel-Crafts acylation, which is an electrophilic substitution on the benzene ring.

Choose the acyl source and catalyst**
To deliver $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^+\text{=O}$, use ethanoyl chloride, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$. Anhydrous aluminium chloride, $\text{AlCl}_3$, acts as a Lewis acid catalyst to generate the electrophile: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COCl} + \text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{C}^+\text{=O} + \text{AlCl}_4^-$$
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ (ethanoyl chloride) with anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$ catalyst.

hints: For $\text{Cl}_2$ with UV light at low temperature, decide whether the benzene ring or the alkyl side chain reacts under radical conditions.
For nitration with conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ / conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, recall how the $\text{COCH}_3$ group activates or deactivates the ring and where it directs the next electrophile.
Think about why bromine water decolourises with phenols and alkenes but not with a simple aryl ketone like phenylethanone.
Match each reactive case to its mechanism name, distinguishing attack by radicals from attack by electrophiles.
Remember only one organic product is needed in each row, so draw mono-substitution at the most favoured position.
walkthrough:
Chlorine with UV attacks the side chain**
UV light splits $\text{Cl}_2$ into $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ radicals. At $10^\circ\text{C}$ the benzene ring is too stable to react, but the $\text{CH}_3$ next to $\text{C=O}$ undergoes free radical substitution of one H by Cl. Product is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_2\text{Cl}$. Chlorine stays in the side chain only, not on the ring.

Nitration goes meta because COCH3 deactivates**
Conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ + conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ generates $\text{NO}_2^+$. The $\text{COCH}_3$ group withdraws electrons and deactivates the ring, and it is meta-directing. So electrophilic substitution gives mainly the 3-nitro isomer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3 \rightarrow$ 3-$\text{O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{COCH}_3$.

Bromine water does nothing**
Bromine water is a test for electron-rich alkenes and activated phenols. Phenylethanone has a deactivated benzene ring and a ketone $\text{C=O}$, neither of which reacts with dilute $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ under these conditions. So write 'no reaction'.

Final answer: With $\text{Cl}_2$/UV: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_2\text{Cl}$, free radical substitution.
With conc. $\text{HNO}_3$/conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$: 3-nitrophenylethanone, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4(\text{NO}_2)\text{COCH}_3$ with $\text{NO}_2$ meta to $\text{COCH}_3$, electrophilic substitution.
With bromine water: no reaction.

hints: Focus on the $\text{C=O}$ bond and the nucleophile $\text{CN}^-$ adding to the electron-poor carbon without any leaving group being expelled.
walkthrough:
Name the carbonyl attack**
$\text{CN}^-$ attacks the $\delta+$ carbon of the polar $\text{C=O}$ and the pi bond breaks to give $\text{O}^-$. No atom leaves, a new $\text{C-C}$ bond simply adds across the double bond, so this is nucleophilic addition.
Final answer: Nucleophilic addition.

hints: Start by showing the polarity of the carbonyl as $\text{C}^{\delta+}$-$\text{O}^{\delta-}$ and where the pi electrons move when attacked.
Identify the nucleophilic atom in $\text{CN}^-$ and where its lone pair attacks.
Draw the resulting alkoxide intermediate $\text{C-O}^-$ and think how it gains $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{HCN}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Show how $\text{CN}^-$ is regenerated so that NaCN acts catalytically.
walkthrough:
Set up the polar carbonyl**
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so label $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ on $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{=O}$. Draw a curly arrow starting in the middle of the $\text{C=O}$ double bond and pointing to O. This shows the pi electrons moving onto oxygen.

Attack by cyanide**
The nucleophile is $:C\equiv N^-$, attacking through carbon. Show a lone pair on that carbon and a curly arrow from it to the carbonyl $\text{C}^{\delta+}$. Together steps 1 and 2 form the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3 + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{O}^-)(\text{CH}_3)(\text{CN})$$

Protonate to give the cyanohydrin and regenerate catalyst**
Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{O}^-$ lone pair to $\text{H}^+$ of $\text{HCN}$ (or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ or H of HCN). At the same time show the $\text{H-CN}$ bond arrow moving onto CN to reform $\text{CN}^-$. The organic product is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{CH}_3)(\text{CN})$, and $\text{CN}^-$ is free to catalyse another cycle.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{C}^{\delta+}$=$\text{O}^{\delta-}$ shown; curly arrow from $\text{C=C}$ pi bond of $\text{C=O}$ to O; lone pair on C of $\text{CN}^-$ shown; curly arrow from $\text{CN}^-$ (C) to carbonyl C to give $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{O}^-)(\text{CH}_3)(\text{CN})$.
Step 2: curly arrow from $\text{O}^-$ lone pair to H of $\text{HCN}$ (or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$); $\text{H-CN}$ bond arrow to $\text{CN}$ to reform $\text{CN}^-$; product $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}(\text{OH})(\text{CH}_3)(\text{CN})$.

hints: Compare phenylethanone $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$ with phenylethene $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH}_2$ and work out what alcohol could dehydrate to that alkene.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from the alkene**
Step 2 will be dehydration of an alcohol to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH}_2$. Removing $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from adjacent carbons means the OH must be on the benzylic carbon. So D is the secondary alcohol $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$.
Final answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$ (1-phenylethanol).

hints: Recall which hydride donor reduces a ketone $\text{C=O}$ to $\text{CH-OH}$ without affecting the benzene ring.
walkthrough:
Pick the hydride reagent**
Step 1 converts ketone to secondary alcohol. That is reduction by hydride, $\text{H}^-$. Use sodium borohydride, $\text{NaBH}_4$, (or lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_4$) followed by aqueous work up.
Final answer: $\text{NaBH}_4$ or $\text{LiAlH}_4$.

hints: Think of the standard strong acid or hot solid oxide that removes $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from an alcohol to form $\text{C=C}$.
walkthrough:
Dehydrate the alcohol**
Step 2 is elimination of water from $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$ to give $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH}_2$. Heat with concentrated sulfuric acid (or concentrated phosphoric acid, or pass over hot aluminium oxide) to achieve acid-catalysed dehydration.
Final answer: Conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (or conc. $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ or hot $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$).

hints: Count unique carbons in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH}_2$ by pairing the equivalent ortho carbons together and the equivalent meta carbons together.
walkthrough:
Count distinct carbons in phenylethene**
Phenylethene is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH}_2$. In the monosubstituted ring there are 4 environments: ipso C attached to $\text{CH=CH}_2$, 2 equivalent ortho C, 2 equivalent meta C, and para C. The two alkene carbons, $\text{CH}$ and $\text{CH}_2$, are different from each other and from the ring. So $4 + 2 = 6$ signals in the C-13 NMR spectrum.
Final answer: 6 peaks.

hints: Sort the carbons of phenylethanone $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$ into three types: ketone $\text{C=O}$, aromatic ring, and alkyl $\text{CH}_3$.
Recall that highly deshielded $\text{C=O}$ appears near 200 ppm, aryl C near 110 to 160 ppm, and alkyl C attached to $\text{C=O}$ near 25 to 50 ppm.
walkthrough:
Assign the most deshielded carbon**
The ketone carbonyl carbon, $\text{C=O}$, is joined to electronegative oxygen and has no shielding, so it appears furthest downfield at about 190 to 220 ppm.

Assign ring versus alkyl carbons**
Carbons in the benzene ring are $sp^2$ and deshielded by the ring current, appearing at about 110 to 160 ppm. The $\text{CH}_3$ carbon next to $\text{C=O}$ is $sp^3$ alkyl and appears much more upfield at about 25 to 50 ppm.
Final answer: Carbonyl C: 190-220 ppm; aromatic / aryl C: 110-160 ppm; methyl ($\text{CH}_3$) C: 25-50 ppm.
